## Today you will be able to

-   Recognize tidy data and turn a wide table into a long one
-   Read an Excel sheet into R and check it for missing values
-   Build a plot with `ggplot2` layer by layer: data, aesthetics, geoms
-   Show groups with color, shape and facets; use a logarithmic axis
-   Draw histograms and save a plot to a file
-   Describe a sample with the median, quartiles and the five-number summary; draw and read boxplots

# Tidy data

## Tidy data: find the problems

Up to 80% of the time of a data analysis goes into getting the data in order. R and `ggplot2` work best with **tidy data**. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| purl: false
#| out-width: "95%"
#| out-height: "86%"
#| fig-cap: "A messy spreadsheet (messy_sheet_example.xlsx): how many problems can you find?"
screenshot_placeholder("images/excel_messy_sheet.png",
                       paste("data/messy_sheet_example.xlsx opened in Excel, whole table visible:",
                             "merged cells, two header rows, groups by cell color, units, missing codes, total row"))
```

## Spreadsheets: what not to do (structure)

\scriptsize

| Don't | Do instead |
|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Merge cells (e.g. one sample ID across two rows) | One value per cell: repeat the ID in every row |
| Put a title or two header rows above the table | One header row; put titles and notes in a separate sheet |
| Put two values in one cell (`12.5 / 13.1`) | One value per cell: a second measurement is a new row |
| Code groups with cell colour | Put the group in its own column (e.g. `pond`); R cannot see colours |
| Add totals or means inside the data | Keep only raw data; calculate summaries in R |

\normalsize

Each row is one observation, each column is one variable.

## Spreadsheets: what not to do (values)

\scriptsize

| Don't | Do instead |
|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Write units in the cells (`16.5 kb`, `38 %`) | Numbers only; the unit goes in the column name (`length_kb`, `gc_percent`) |
| Mix formats in one column (`38%`, `0.37`, `37.9`) | One format per column |
| Use several codes for missing (`no data`, `n/a`, `-`, `0`) | One code: `NA` or an empty cell. Never `0`: 0 is a value |
| Spell categories differently (`Pond A`, `pond a`, `B`) | One spelling for each category |
| Mix date formats (`02.11.2026`, `Nov 3`, `4/11`) | One format: `2026-11-04` (year-month-day) |
| Use a decimal comma (`10,9`) | A decimal point (`10.9`) |
| Type gene names into Excel without checking | Excel turns some gene names into dates (`SEPT2` -> `2-Sep`): format the column as text |

\normalsize

# Wide and long format

Remember the count matrix from last time? A **read count** is the number of sequencing reads that map to a gene: more reads means more expression.

```{r}
counts <- matrix(c(1520, 980, 12, 1385, 1043, 30, 1610, 875, 7),
                 nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
rownames(counts) <- c("ACTB", "GAPDH", "MYC")
colnames(counts) <- c("sample_1", "sample_2", "sample_3")
counts_wide <- data.frame(gene = rownames(counts), counts)
counts_wide
```

The gene names are now both row names (left) and a column, `gene`. Functions like `pivot_longer()` and `ggplot()` use only columns.

-   **Wide format**: one row per gene, one column of counts per sample. Count tables usually arrive like this.
-   **Long format**: one row per measurement (gene + sample + count). `ggplot2` and most statistical functions need it.

## From wide to long: pivot_longer()

`pivot_longer()` from the `tidyr` package (part of the tidyverse) turns columns into rows. Its arguments:

-   `cols`: which columns to turn into rows. `-gene` means "all columns except `gene`": the minus excludes a column.
-   `names_to`: the name of the new column that gets the old column names (here, the sample names).
-   `values_to`: the name of the new column that gets the values (here, the counts).

Each gene appears once for each sample: 3 genes × 3 samples = 9 rows. `pivot_wider()` does the reverse.

## pivot_longer(): the long table

```{r}
library(tidyr)
counts_long <- pivot_longer(counts_wide, cols = -gene,
                            names_to = "sample", values_to = "count")
counts_long
```

## Your turn 1: wide to long

Read counts (made-up) of three genes in two control samples and two heat-stressed samples. *ACTB* and *GAPDH*, the housekeeping genes, stay stable. *HSPA1A* codes for HSP70, a heat-shock protein: cells make much more of it when they are stressed by heat.

```{r}
heat_counts <- data.frame(gene = c("ACTB", "GAPDH", "HSPA1A"),
                          ctrl_1 = c(1490, 1012, 38),
                          ctrl_2 = c(1532, 968, 45),
                          heat_1 = c(1475, 1001, 1842),
                          heat_2 = c(1508, 990, 2115))
```

1.  Turn `heat_counts` into a long table `heat_long` with the columns `gene`, `sample` and `count`.
2.  How many rows does `heat_long` have, and why?

## Your turn 1: answers

```{r}
heat_long <- pivot_longer(heat_counts, cols = -gene,
                          names_to = "sample", values_to = "count")
heat_long
nrow(heat_long)  # 3 genes x 4 samples = 12
```

```{r}
#| student: true
#| include: false
#| eval: false
heat_long <- pivot_longer(___, cols = -___,
                          names_to = ___, values_to = ___)
heat_long
___(heat_long)
```

# Our data: organelle genomes

## Organelle genomes from NCBI RefSeq

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
genomes_chk <- readxl::read_excel("data/organelle_genomes.xlsx", sheet = "genomes", skip = 1, na = "NA")
map <- read.csv("data/mito_map_human.csv")
```

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
\footnotesize

`organelle_genomes.xlsx`: `r nrow(genomes_chk)` complete genomes from NCBI RefSeq, 25 per group: mitochondria of 5 groups and plastids of land plants.

\scriptsize

| Column | What it is |
|:-------------|:------------------------|
| `accession` | RefSeq number(s) |
| `organism` | species name |
| `group` | group of organisms |
| `organelle` | mitochondrion, plastid |
| `length_kb` | genome length, kb |
| `gc_percent` | GC content, % |
| `protein_genes` | protein-coding genes |
| `trna_genes` | tRNA genes |
| `note` | unusual records |

\footnotesize

NCBI gives lengths in bp; 1 kb = 1,000 bp, 1 Mb = 1,000 kb.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| purl: false
#| fig-width: 3.2
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "The human mitogenome (NC_012920.1): genes on the two DNA strands."
map$ring <- ifelse(map$strand == "+", 2.2, 1.2)
ggplot(map) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = ring, ymax = ring + 0.8, fill = type),
            color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_text(data = map[map$type != "tRNA", ],
            aes(x = (start + end) / 2, y = ring + 1.4, label = gene), size = 2.3) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -1.5, label = "16,569 bp", size = 3.3) +
  coord_polar() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 16569)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1.5, 4.4)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("protein-coding" = "#4C9BE8", rRNA = "#E8A33D", tRNA = "grey40"),
                    name = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::
:::::

\tiny O'Leary N.A. et al. (2016). Reference sequence (RefSeq) database at NCBI. *Nucleic Acids Research* 44: D733–D745.

## Reading an Excel sheet

Save `organelle_genomes.xlsx` into the `data` folder of your project. The package `readxl` (installed with the tidyverse) reads Excel files:

```{r}
library(readxl)
genomes <- read_excel("data/organelle_genomes.xlsx",
                      sheet = "genomes", # sheet name
                      skip = 1,          # skip the "Source" row
                      na = "NA")         # code for missing values
```

-   Without `skip = 1`, R would take the "Source: ..." row as column names.
-   Without `na = "NA"`, the text `"NA"` would turn the number columns into text.

## Checking the data

```{r}
str(genomes)
```

`read_excel()` returns a tibble. `group` and `organelle` are text (`chr`); turn them into factors:

```{r}
genomes$group <- factor(genomes$group)
genomes$organelle <- factor(genomes$organelle)
```

## Unusual records: the note column

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
noted <- genomes[!is.na(genomes$note), ]
summed <- noted[grepl("^summed", noted$note), ]
```

`r nrow(noted)` records have a `note`. Read it before you analyse the data:

-   Split genomes: in `r paste0("*", summed$organism, "*", collapse = ", ")`, the mitogenome is split into several chromosomes. Each species is one row: the lengths are summed.
-   Missing annotation: some records lack tRNA genes or annotate only part of the genome (next slides).
-   Unusual counts: two records have more tRNA genes than their relatives; the note says why (later today).

```{r}
genomes[!is.na(genomes$note), c("organism", "note")]
```

## Missing values: counting them

`is.na()` returns `TRUE` for each missing value; `sum()` of a logical vector counts the `TRUE` values:

```{r}
sum(is.na(genomes$trna_genes))
```

`summary()` describes each column; for numeric columns it also counts the `NA`'s:

```{r}
summary(genomes[, c("length_kb", "gc_percent", "protein_genes", "trna_genes")])
```

## Missing values: which rows?

`complete.cases()` returns `TRUE` for each row without any `NA`:

```{r}
nrow(genomes[!complete.cases(genomes), ])
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
n_no_note <- sum(is.na(genomes$note))
```

Too many: `note` is empty (`NA`) in `r n_no_note` rows, and an empty note is not missing data. Check only the measurement columns:

```{r}
num_cols <- c("length_kb", "gc_percent", "protein_genes", "trna_genes")
genomes[!complete.cases(genomes[, num_cols]), c("organism", "protein_genes", "trna_genes")]
```

## Why each value is missing

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
na_rec <- genomes[!complete.cases(genomes[, num_cols]), ]
na_lines <- paste0("-   *", na_rec$organism, "* (", na_rec$group, ", ", na_rec$organelle, "): ", na_rec$note, ".")
```

The `note` column gives the reason for each record:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| purl: false
cat(na_lines, sep = "\n")
```

Two different reasons:

-   The annotation is missing: the genes exist, but the record does not list them.
-   Only part of the genome is annotated (the cucumber: 1 of its 3 chromosomes): a count would be too low.

In both cases the true number is unknown, so it is `NA`.

## NA is not 0

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
anemonia <- genomes[genomes$organism == "Anemonia sulcata", ]
cnid_chk <- genomes[genomes$group == "cnidarians", ]
```

The record of the sea anemone *Anemonia sulcata* (`r anemonia$accession`) lists `r anemonia$protein_genes` protein-coding genes but no tRNA genes, while `r sum(cnid_chk$trna_genes %in% 1:2)` of the `r nrow(cnid_chk)` cnidarians in the table have 1 or 2. "Not annotated" does not mean "no genes". What if we wrote 0 instead of `NA`?

```{r}
cnid <- genomes[genomes$group == "cnidarians", ]
mean(cnid$trna_genes, na.rm = TRUE)  # NA left out
trna_zero <- cnid$trna_genes
trna_zero[is.na(trna_zero)] <- 0     # wrong: NA written as 0
mean(trna_zero)
```

Writing 0 for a missing value changes every statistic you calculate. `na.rm = TRUE` leaves the `NA` out instead.

# Plots with ggplot2

## Last time: quick-look plots in base R

At the end of the last session we drew two quick plots of `genes.csv`:

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
genes <- read.csv("data/genes.csv")
hist(genes$length_bp)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
plot(x = genes$length_bp,
     y = genes$n_exons)
```
:::
:::::

## The same plots with ggplot2

`ggplot2` is a package from the tidyverse for publication-quality plots. Load it before the first plot:

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = genes,
       aes(x = length_bp)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 5)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
ggplot(data = genes,
       aes(x = length_bp,
           y = n_exons)) +
  geom_point()
```
:::
:::::

## How ggplot2 builds a plot

A ggplot is built from layers joined with `+`:

-   `ggplot(data = genes)`: the data, a data frame (one column per variable).
-   `aes(x = length_bp, y = n_exons)`: the **aesthetics**: which variable goes on which visual property (x, y, color, shape, size).
-   `geom_point()`: the **geom**, the kind of object that draws the data (points, bars, boxes, lines).
-   More layers change the look: axis labels, colors, themes, panels.

The idea comes from the "grammar of graphics" (Wilkinson 2005): every plot is data + aesthetics + geoms. `ggplot2` (gg = grammar of graphics) puts it into R.

Wickham H. (2016). *ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis*. Springer. Free online: <https://ggplot2-book.org>.

## A first scatterplot

A **scatterplot** shows two numeric variables: genome length on x, GC content on y.

```{r}
#| opts.label: "wide"
ggplot(data = genomes, aes(x = length_kb, y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_point()
```

Almost all points are squeezed against the left side.

## Logarithms

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
len_range <- range(genomes$length_kb)
```

The **logarithm** log10 answers "10 to what power gives this number?": $10^1 = 10$, $10^2 = 100$, $10^3 = 1000$, so log10(100) = 2 and log10(1000) = 3.

```{r}
10^2
log10(c(10, 100, 1000))
log10(c(16, 160, 1600))  # each 10 times longer: +1
```

A step of 1 in log10 means "10 times more". Our genome lengths go from `r len_range[1]` to `r len_range[2]` kb, so their log10 goes only from `r round(log10(len_range[1]), 2)` to `r round(log10(len_range[2]), 2)`.

## Why a logarithmic scale?

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
animal_range <- range(genomes$length_kb[genomes$group %in% c("vertebrates", "insects", "cnidarians")])
```

The largest genome is about `r round(len_range[2] / len_range[1])` times the smallest. On a normal axis, all animal mitogenomes (`r animal_range[1]` to `r animal_range[2]` kb) are squeezed into one corner. On a **logarithmic scale**, each step multiplies the value by 10 (10, 100, 1000 kb): small and large genomes get the same amount of space.

```{r}
#| opts.label: "wide"
ggplot(data = genomes, aes(x = length_kb, y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10()
```

## Transform the data or the axis?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Transform the data: the axis shows log10 values.

```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
ggplot(genomes,
       aes(x = log10(length_kb),
           y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_point()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Transform the axis: the labels stay in kb.

```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
ggplot(genomes,
       aes(x = length_kb,
           y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10()
```
:::
:::::

The points are in the same places. For plots, `scale_x_log10()` is easier to read: 2.0 on the left plot means 100 kb.

## Themes

A theme changes the look of the plot, but not the data. Try `theme_bw()`, `theme_classic()`, `theme_minimal()`:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(data = genomes, aes(x = length_kb, y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  theme_classic()
```

`theme_set()` makes a theme the default for all plots in this R session (`base_size` sets the font size):

```{r}
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 14))
```

## Axis labels and title

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
ggplot(data = genomes, aes(x = length_kb, y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Genome length, kb (log scale)", y = "GC content, %",
       title = "Organelle genomes:\nlength and GC content") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))  # center the title
```

`\n` starts a new line in a label.

## Point size, color and shape

Settings outside `aes()` apply to all points:

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
ggplot(genomes, aes(x = length_kb,
                    y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_point(size = 1,
             color = "blue") +
  scale_x_log10()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
ggplot(genomes, aes(x = length_kb,
                    y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_point(shape = 22, size = 2,
             color = "red",
             fill = "yellow") +
  scale_x_log10()
```
:::
:::::

`shape` is a number from 0 to 25 (`?points`); shapes 21–25 have both an outline (`color`) and a `fill`.

## A plot as an object; saving a plot

A plot can be stored in a variable and changed later:

```{r}
gc_plot <- ggplot(genomes, aes(x = length_kb, y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10()
gc_plot <- gc_plot + labs(x = "Genome length, kb (log scale)", y = "GC content, %")
```

`ggsave()` saves a plot to a file. The file type comes from the extension: `.png` for slides and documents, `.pdf` for print (it stays sharp at any size).

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| script: "comment"
ggsave("gc_plot.png", plot = gc_plot, width = 15, height = 10, units = "cm", dpi = 300)
ggsave("gc_plot.pdf", plot = gc_plot, width = 15, height = 10, units = "cm")
```

The files appear in your project folder and in the `Files` pane.

# Aesthetics

## Mapping a variable to color

Inside `aes()`, `color` shows a **variable**: each organelle gets its own color, and a legend appears.

```{r}
#| opts.label: "wide"
ggplot(genomes, aes(x = length_kb, y = gc_percent, color = organelle)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10()
```

Outside `aes()`, `color = "blue"` is a **setting**: the same color for all points.

## Overlapping points

Many points lie on top of each other (e.g. the plastids), so you cannot see how many there are. Three fixes: smaller points (`size`), see-through points (`alpha`, from 0 to 1), and points with a black outline and a colored `fill` (`shape = 21`):

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
ggplot(genomes, aes(x = length_kb,
                    y = gc_percent,
                    color = organelle)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
ggplot(genomes, aes(x = length_kb,
                    y = gc_percent,
                    fill = organelle)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21,
             color = "black",
             size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10()
```
:::
:::::

From now on, scatterplots use this style. With `shape = 21`, the variable goes to `fill`, not `color`.

## Choosing your own colors

`scale_fill_manual()` gives one color per group (`scale_color_manual()` does the same for `color`). The colors go to the groups in alphabetical order: `mitochondrion`, then `plastid`.

```{r}
#| opts.label: "wide"
org_plot <- ggplot(genomes, aes(x = length_kb, y = gc_percent,
                                fill = organelle)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, color = "black", size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "forestgreen"))
org_plot
```

R knows `r length(colors())` color names (`colors()`), or use codes like `"#1B9E77"`.

## Legend position

`theme(legend.position = ...)`: `"right"` (default), `"bottom"`, `"top"`, `"left"`, `"none"` (no legend), or `"inside"` the plot area:

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
org_plot +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
org_plot +
  theme(legend.position = "inside",
        legend.position.inside = c(0.85, 0.2))
```
:::
:::::

`legend.position.inside = c(0.85, 0.2)`: the position as a fraction of the plot width and height, from the bottom left corner.

## Two variables: fill and shape

<!-- OPTIONAL -->

`shape` can show a second variable. `scale_shape_manual()` picks shapes that have a fill (21: circle, 24: triangle):

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(genomes, aes(x = length_kb, y = gc_percent,
                    fill = group, shape = organelle)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(21, 24)) +
  scale_x_log10()
```

Two legends, 6 combinations: possible, but hard to read. Facets are often better.

## Comparing organisms: mitochondria only

To compare organisms, we compare the same kind of genome: mitochondria. Plastids exist only in plants, so a "land plants" group with both organelles would mix two kinds of genomes.

Keep only the rows where `organelle` is `"mitochondrion"`:

```{r}
mito <- genomes[genomes$organelle == "mitochondrion", ]
nrow(mito)
```

## Facets

A **facet** is a small panel with one group of the data. `facet_wrap(~ group)` draws one panel per group, with the same axes:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.7
ggplot(mito, aes(x = length_kb, y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, color = "black", fill = "grey60",
             size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ group)
```

## Facets in a grid

<!-- OPTIONAL -->

`facet_grid(rows ~ columns)`: one panel for each combination of two variables (here all genomes, both organelles).

```{r}
#| opts.label: "wide"
ggplot(genomes, aes(x = length_kb, y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, color = "black", fill = "grey60",
             size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_grid(organelle ~ group)
```

Most panels in the plastid row are empty: only land plants have plastids.

# Distributions

## Histogram

A **histogram** shows how often values fall into intervals (bins). `binwidth` sets the width of a bin:

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
ggplot(genomes,
       aes(x = gc_percent)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| opts.label: "S"
ggplot(genomes,
       aes(x = gc_percent)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1)
```
:::
:::::

Wide bins hide details; very narrow bins show mostly noise. Try a few widths.

## Geoms and stats

A histogram first counts the values in each bin (a statistical step, a "stat") and then draws bars (a geom). The same counts can be drawn by another geom: `stat_bin()` with `geom = "line"`.

```{r}
#| opts.label: "wide"
ggplot(genomes, aes(x = gc_percent)) +
  stat_bin(geom = "line", binwidth = 2, linewidth = 1, color = "red")
```

`linewidth` sets the thickness of lines; `size` sets the size of points.

## Comparing groups

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
Facets one above the other (`ncol = 1`) share the x axis, so the groups are easy to compare (mitochondria only):

```{r}
#| fig-show: "hide"
ggplot(mito, aes(
  x = gc_percent)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ group,
             ncol = 1)
```
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| purl: false
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 5.2
ggplot(mito, aes(x = gc_percent)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10)  # smaller font: tall plot in a column
```
:::
:::::

## Density curves

<!-- OPTIONAL -->

A density curve is a smooth version of a histogram. `fill` colors the area; `alpha` makes it see-through:

```{r}
#| opts.label: "wide"
ggplot(genomes, aes(x = gc_percent, fill = organelle)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)
```

## Group means

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
n_big <- sum(mito$length_kb > 1000)
```

`stat_summary()` calculates a statistic for each group and draws it with a geom; `fun = "mean"` gives the mean:

```{r}
#| opts.label: "wide"
ggplot(mito, aes(x = group, y = gc_percent, fill = group)) +
  stat_summary(fun = "mean", geom = "bar")
```

The bars show mean GC%, not mean genome length: lengths are very skewed (`r n_big` plant mitogenome`r if (n_big > 1) "s are" else " is"` over 1000 kb), so a mean length would mislead. The median, later today, handles this.

## A trend line

<!-- OPTIONAL -->

`geom_smooth(method = "lm")` adds a straight line fitted to the points: a linear model, the topic of Nov 9.

```{r}
#| opts.label: "wide"
ggplot(genomes, aes(x = length_kb, y = protein_genes)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, color = "black", fill = "grey60",
             size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

# Describing a sample

## Population and sample

-   **Population**: all the objects you want to draw conclusions about, e.g. all insect mitochondrial genomes.
-   **Sample**: the objects you actually measured, e.g. our 25 insect mitogenomes (RefSeq has about 5,000).
-   **Descriptive statistics** summarise the sample: where its values are (center) and how far they spread.
-   Later in the course we will use samples to draw conclusions about populations.

## Types of data

\scriptsize

| Type | Values | In our table |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------|
| Categorical | categories (groups), no numbers | `group`, `organelle` |
| Discrete numeric | counts: whole numbers | `protein_genes`, `trna_genes` |
| Continuous numeric | measurements: any value in a range | `length_kb`, `gc_percent` |

\normalsize

Describing numeric data needs two kinds of numbers:

-   Center: the **median** (`r zh(gl02, "Median")`) today, the mean on Nov 6
-   Spread: the quartiles today, the standard deviation on Nov 6

## Median

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
ins_l <- mito$length_kb[mito$group == "insects"]
s8 <- sort(head(ins_l, 8))
```

The **median** is the middle value of the sorted data. The lengths of the first 8 insect mitogenomes:

```{r}
insects <- mito[mito$group == "insects", ]
sizes <- head(insects$length_kb, 8)
sizes
sort(sizes)
```

With an odd number of values, the median is the middle one. With an even number (here 8), it is the mean of the two middle values: the 4th (`r s8[4]`) and the 5th (`r s8[5]`).

```{r}
median(sizes)
```

## The median is robust to outliers

Suppose the cucumber mitogenome (1684.6 kb) ended up in the insect table by mistake:

```{r}
sizes2 <- c(sizes, 1684.6)
median(sizes)
median(sizes2)
mean(sizes)
mean(sizes2)
```

One extreme value moves the mean from `r round(mean(sizes), 1)` to `r round(mean(sizes2), 1)` kb, but the median only from `r median(sizes)` to `r median(sizes2)` kb. An extreme value like this is an **outlier** (`r zh(gl02, "Outlier")`).

## Quantiles

A **quantile** (`r zh(gl02, "Quantile")`) splits the sorted data into parts with the same number of values in each:

-   the median splits the data into 2 parts;
-   the **quartiles** (`r zh(gl02, "Quartile")`) split it into 4 parts: 25% of the values are below Q1, 50% below Q2 (= the median), 75% below Q3;
-   the percentiles split it into 100 parts: e.g. 10% of the values are below the 10th percentile.

`quantile()` calculates them; `probs` gives the proportions:

```{r}
quantile(insects$length_kb, probs = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
quantile(insects$length_kb, probs = c(0.1, 0.9))
```

## Five-number summary

`quantile()` without `probs` returns the **five-number summary**: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.

```{r}
quantile(insects$length_kb)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
q <- quantile(insects$length_kb)
```

Half of the insect mitogenomes are between `r q[2]` and `r q[4]` kb long. This range, $Q_3 - Q_1$ = `r round(q[4] - q[2], 2)` kb, is the **interquartile range** (`r zh(gl02, "Interquartile range (IQR)")`), IQR for short: the spread of the middle 50% of the values.

## Boxplot: the five-number summary as a picture

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
iqr <- q[4] - q[2]
upper_w <- max(insects$length_kb[insects$length_kb <= q[4] + 1.5 * iqr])
lower_w <- min(insects$length_kb[insects$length_kb >= q[2] - 1.5 * iqr])
n_out <- sum(insects$length_kb > q[4] + 1.5 * iqr | insects$length_kb < q[2] - 1.5 * iqr)
```

::::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| purl: false
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(insects, aes(x = 1, y = length_kb)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.27, y = c(q[2], q[4], upper_w),
           label = c("Q1", "Q3", "whisker"),
           hjust = 0, size = 4.5, color = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.73, y = c(q[3], lower_w), label = c("median", "whisker"),
           hjust = 1, size = 4.5, color = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.08, y = max(insects$length_kb), label = "outlier",
           hjust = 0, size = 4.5, color = "grey30") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.25, 1.75)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Genome length, kb") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
A **boxplot** (`r zh(gl02, "Boxplot")`) of the insect mitogenome lengths:

-   the line in the box: the median;
-   the box: from Q1 to Q3, so its height is the IQR;
-   the whiskers: to the most extreme values that are within 1.5 × IQR of the box;
-   points beyond the whiskers: possible outliers, drawn one by one (here `r n_out`).

The whiskers reach the minimum and the maximum only when there are no outliers.
:::
:::::

## A boxplot in ggplot2

`geom_boxplot()` needs a numeric variable on y; on x, a group or a text label:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "45%"
ggplot(insects, aes(x = "insects", y = length_kb)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Genome length, kb")
```

## Summaries by group with the pipe

`dplyr` (part of the tidyverse) calculates summaries for each group:

```{r}
library(dplyr)
```

-   The **pipe** `%>%` passes the result on its left into the next function: read it as "and then". `x %>% f()` is the same as `f(x)`.
-   `group_by()`: split the table into groups; `summarise()`: one row of summaries per group; `n()`: the number of rows in a group.
-   R also has its own pipe, `|>`, which works the same way; in this course we use `%>%`.
-   `library(tidyverse)` loads `ggplot2`, `dplyr`, `tidyr` and the other tidyverse packages at once.

## Summaries by group: a first example

How many genomes of each kind do we have, and how long are they?

```{r}
#| message: true
genomes %>%
  group_by(group, organelle) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), median_length = round(median(length_kb)))
```

This is a message, not an error: R tells you the result is still grouped.

## Boxplots by group

```{r}
#| opts.label: "wide"
ggplot(mito, aes(x = group, y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "GC content, %")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
med_gc <- tapply(mito$gc_percent, as.character(mito$group), median)
```

Insect mitogenomes are AT-rich (median GC `r med_gc[["insects"]]`%), vertebrate mitogenomes are not (`r med_gc[["vertebrates"]]`%), although both are about 16 kb long.

```{r}
#| include: false

trna_sum <- mito %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(Q1 = quantile(trna_genes, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
```

## An outlier: biology or error?

<!-- OPTIONAL -->

```{r}
cnid[cnid$trna_genes > 2 & !is.na(cnid$trna_genes), c("organism", "accession", "trna_genes")]
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
stony <- c("Acropora horrida", "Agaricia humilis", "Fungiacyathus stephanus",
           "Gardineria hawaiiensis", "Pocillopora damicornis", "Siderastrea radians")
stony_trna <- unique(cnid$trna_genes[cnid$organism %in% stony])
stopifnot(all(stony %in% cnid$organism), length(stony_trna) == 1)
```

*Porites lutea* is a stony (scleractinian) coral. The other `r length(stony)` stony corals in the table have `r stony_trna` tRNA genes, as is usual for this group. A real gain of tRNA genes, or an error in the annotation?

-   Do not delete a point only because it is far from the others: an outlier can be real biology.
-   Check the source: open the record (`NC_029695.1` in NCBI Nucleotide) and see how the tRNA genes were found.
-   Compare with related species, and keep a note of what you decided: here, `note` says "possible annotation error".

## Median and quartiles describe any distribution

<!-- OPTIONAL -->

-   The median and the quartiles do not assume any particular shape of the distribution: they work for symmetric or skewed data, with outliers or without.
-   They hardly react to outliers, so they are a safe first summary of any sample.

# Summary

## Key terms

\scriptsize

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| purl: false
key_terms("glossary/02_intro_ggplot_glossary.md",
          c("Tidy data", "Aesthetic", "Geom", "Facet", "Logarithmic scale",
            "Median", "Five-number summary", "Boxplot"))
```

## What we have learned

-   **Tidy data**: one variable per column, one observation per row, one value per cell. `pivot_longer()` turns a wide table into a long one.
-   `read_excel()` reads a sheet; check it with `str()`, `summary()` and `complete.cases()`. A missing value is `NA`, not 0.
-   A ggplot is built from layers: data + **aesthetics** (`aes()`) + **geoms**, joined with `+`. Show groups with color, fill, shape or facets; a logarithmic scale shows small and very large values on one axis.
-   The **median** and the **quartiles** describe a sample and are robust to **outliers**; the **five-number summary** is shown by a **boxplot**.
-   `%>%`, `group_by()` and `summarise()` calculate summaries for each group.

## Key R functions: data

\scriptsize

| Function | What it does | Example |
|---------------|-----------------|--------------------|
| `pivot_longer()` | (`tidyr`) Wide table to long table; `cols`: columns to turn into rows (`-gene`: all except `gene`); `names_to`, `values_to`: names of the new columns | `pivot_longer(counts_wide, cols = -gene, names_to = "sample", values_to = "count")` |
| `read_excel()` | (`readxl`) Reads an Excel sheet; `skip`: rows above the header; `na`: code for missing values | `read_excel("data/x.xlsx", skip = 1, na = "NA")` |
| `is.na()` | `TRUE` for each missing value | `sum(is.na(genomes$trna_genes))` |
| `summary()` | Summary of each column, with the number of `NA`'s | `summary(genomes)` |
| `complete.cases()` | `TRUE` for each row without `NA` | `genomes[!complete.cases(genomes), ]` |
| `log10()` | Logarithm to base 10 | `log10(100)` |

## Key R functions: ggplot2

\scriptsize

| Function | What it does | Example |
|---------------|-----------------|--------------------|
| `ggplot()`, `aes()` | Start a plot: the data and the aesthetics | `ggplot(genomes, aes(x = length_kb, y = gc_percent))` |
| `geom_point()` | Scatterplot; `shape = 21` + `fill`, `alpha` against overlap | `geom_point(shape = 21, fill = "grey", alpha = 0.6)` |
| `scale_x_log10()` | Logarithmic x axis | `scale_x_log10()` |
| `labs()` | Axis labels and title | `labs(x = "Length, kb", title = "...")` |
| `theme_bw()`, `theme_set()` | A theme; make it the default | `theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 14))` |
| `theme()` | Changes parts of the look, e.g. the legend | `theme(legend.position = "bottom")` |
| `scale_fill_manual()` | Your own colors for groups (`scale_color_manual()` for `color`) | `scale_fill_manual(values = c("red", "blue"))` |
| `facet_wrap()`, `facet_grid()` | One panel per group | `facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 1)` |
| `ggsave()` | Saves a plot to a file | `ggsave("plot.png", plot = p, width = 15, height = 10, units = "cm")` |

## Key R functions: distributions

\scriptsize

| Function | What it does | Example |
|---------------|-----------------|--------------------|
| `geom_histogram()` | Histogram; `binwidth` sets the bin width | `geom_histogram(binwidth = 1)` |
| `stat_bin()` | Counts values in bins, drawn with any geom | `stat_bin(geom = "line", binwidth = 2)` |
| `geom_density()` | Density curve | `geom_density(alpha = 0.5)` |
| `stat_summary()` | A statistic for each group, drawn with a geom | `stat_summary(fun = "mean", geom = "bar")` |
| `geom_smooth()` | A fitted line; `method = "lm"`: a straight line | `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` |
| `scale_shape_manual()` | Your own shapes for groups | `scale_shape_manual(values = c(21, 24))` |

## Key R functions: descriptive statistics

\scriptsize

| Function | What it does | Example |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------|
| `sort()` | Sorts values from smallest to largest | `sort(sizes)` |
| `median()` | Median; `na.rm = TRUE` ignores NA | `median(x, na.rm = TRUE)` |
| `quantile()` | Quantiles; without `probs`: the five-number summary | `quantile(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.75))` |
| `geom_boxplot()` | Boxplot | `ggplot(mito, aes(x = group, y = gc_percent)) + geom_boxplot()` |
| `%>%` | Pipe: passes the result on to the next function | `genomes %>% group_by(group)` |
| `group_by()` | (`dplyr`) Splits a table into groups | `group_by(group, organelle)` |
| `summarise()` | (`dplyr`) One row of summaries per group | `summarise(median = median(gc_percent))` |
| `n()` | (`dplyr`) Number of rows in a group, inside `summarise()` | `summarise(n = n())` |
